Ah, so you're saying the scrambled signal could be uploaded by my phone, and it would still be possible for TPTB to decode if it became important enough.

Kind of.

GPS works on "trilateration", figuring out what the distance is between you and each of several satellites, where the distance is determined by measuring the difference in timing of a clock signal that is sent from each satellite.

If the people running the satellites were to screw with the clock signals, then your GPS device will have the wrong location.

If the clock signals were screwed with according to let's say a specific pattern, but that pattern is known only to the people doing to screwing, then you would get a nonsense location. But when your device reports its location to Google or whoever via your Map app, it would be trivial for them, if they know the error that was applied, to subtract that error signal back out and get your true location.

To grossly oversimplify it let's say the signal were fudged as follows. We could call this a sort of "one time pad":

  • From 12:00 PM until 12:01 PM adjust by 100 feet north
  • From 12:01 PM until 12:02 PM adjust by 50 feet east
  • From 12:02 PM until 12:03 PM adjust by 30 feet south ... and so on

If you are looking at your GPS you will have no idea where you are.

But if you are the person fudging the signal then you just subtract these error values from the location that the target is reporting, and you will know where he is.

It's not a matter of "if it's important enough"... if this were the sort of scheme being done then they would just know. It is only arithmetic to reverse the scrambling.

Now really it's not quite as simple as I said because what is really being scrambled are the clock signals, they would be adding "jitter" probably. But that is a lot more to explain. I'm not really an expert on GPS anyway so if someone who knows more would like to chime in please do.
